A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. The complete appendices—A–E in v1 and A–D in v2—support reliable comparison, including identification of relocated and removed material.

before.justification: v1 reports original model hierarchy analyses, demographic emotion-recognition experiments, a 60-participant human study, and evaluations involving wine aromas and GoEmotions.

after.justification: v2 retains original model and human-study results and adds Mistral training-status comparisons and hierarchy evaluations using GoEmotions, DeepSeek-R1 variants, and alternative prompts.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix B retain the matching matrix C = Y^T Y and the same thresholded, asymmetric parent–child rules. Testing additional models, including an existing RL-fine-tuned checkpoint, does not change the proposed hierarchy-construction method.

E1.justification: GoEmotions remains covered, but its evaluated task shifts from comparing human labels with neutral, female, and Black persona classifications in v1 Appendix E to hierarchy reconstruction across model sizes in v2 Figure 11. Synthetic emotion scenarios, wine aromas, and the human study remain covered.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 9 introduces a comparison between base Mistral-7B and an RL-fine-tuned Mistral-7B variant, absent from v1. The existing hierarchical-clustering comparison is retained as v1 Figure 11 and v2 Figure 14.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation conditions involving base versus RL-fine-tuned Mistral-7B, 32B/70B DeepSeek-R1 variants, and an alternative extraction prompt. Figure 17 also reports constructing persona hierarchies from 5,000 scenarios and evaluating accuracy on 2,700 additional scenarios; v1 linked this analysis to Figure 21's 2,700-scenario hierarchies. This substantially expands the evaluation design and revises a reported protocol, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks of dependence on synthetic scenarios, model family, and prompt wording through GoEmotions hierarchies, DeepSeek-R1 variants, and an emotion-to-sentiment prompt substitution. It also tests recognition differences associated with RL fine-tuning. Conversely, v1's detailed multi-persona confusion diagrams, displayed persona-tree case studies, and GoEmotions demographic-bias analysis are removed; aggregate persona analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds a McNemar test for the Mistral surprise-recognition comparison, reporting chi-square(1) = 6.40 and p = 0.011. Existing correlation significance reporting remains, and neither version supplies repeated-run or seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds Mistral recognition results, including 20.0% versus 33.3% surprise accuracy for base and RL-fine-tuned models, and new GoEmotions, DeepSeek-R1, and alternative-prompt hierarchies. Detailed results in v1 Figures 16, 21, and 22 are removed. Appendix D also corrects the stated cluster-distance correlations from 0.55/0.73/0.47 to 0.38/0.64/0.51, matching the values already plotted in v1 Figure 13 and retained in v2 Figure 16.

T1.justification: The probabilistic assumptions, joint and conditional probability derivations in Appendix A, and generalized classification formulation in Appendix B are unchanged. The corrected attribution of the emotion-word list does not alter the mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and discussion retain the central claims about hierarchical organization emerging with scale, alignment with human psychology, and demographic recognition biases. The claim that RL helps surprise recognition already appeared in v1's discussion; v2 supplies supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 develops a more explicit prediction-error explanation for why RL might improve surprise recognition and interprets its new robustness checks as evidence of broader applicability. It removes v1's unsupported 'Experiment 5' assertion linking emotion recognition directly to persuasion and manipulation. The substantive limitations otherwise remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly describes the retained human sample's demographic composition, including ages 18–71 and 32 men/28 women, and documents the Mistral variants' training provenance and alternative prompt wording. It omits v1's interactive emotion-wheel demo link. Existing generation prompts, NNsight usage, and NetworkX information remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the RL/surprise interpretation and additional models, including Itti and Baldi, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1, and the Sotopia works. Fischer and Bidell is removed, and Appendix A correctly attributes the emotion list to Shaver et al. The main related-work positioning remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized prose corrections and introductory additions, changed author and affiliation text, author–year citations, and new acknowledgements. The geometry–accuracy discussion moves into Appendix D, and the standalone GoEmotions appendix disappears. Most existing explanatory prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, with extensive figure resizing and repositioning. v2 adds Figures 9 and 11–13, combines v1 Figures 6 and 14 into Figure 17, and removes v1 Figures 16, 21, and 22. Several captions and panel references are corrected.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the hierarchy claim with real-comment, reasoning-model, and prompt-variation checks, and supplies concrete evidence for the previously unsupported RL-surprise statement. Corrected correlation reporting and added participant details also improve reliability and transparency. The net gain is limited by the largely qualitative robustness evidence and removal of v1's GoEmotions persona-bias validation and detailed persona analyses.
